new_statements.quote: There is very little textual evidence as to how Cornish was stressed. Evidence from place-names suggests that the pattern was the same as in Breton (though not the Gwenedeg dialect thereof). [...] Unpublished work by Keith Bailey on stress in Middle Cornish verse suggests that, as in Welsh, the stress-accent was usually on the penultimate syllable, but the pitch-accent remained on the ultimate. [...] Normal stress in polysyllables. The primary stress fell on the penultimate syllable, and a secondary stress fell on the fourth and sixth syllables from the end. This applied to most polysyllables, including close compounds.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog stress placement coded per word length as 10 010 1010 01010 101010 0101010 10101010 (1 = a stressed syllable) (src StressTyp2) encodes primary penult plus secondary on every second syllable leftward (4th, 6th from the end) — exactly George's statement 'primary stress fell on the penultimate syllable, and a secondary stress fell on the fourth and sixth syllables from the end'. George adds the exception classes and the pitch accent-on-ultimate remark, which the catalog does not carry. NB: the listed open_url was a wrong item (Gutenberg ballads); the real chapter was located via archive.org search.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of polysyllables (including close compounds); secondary stress on the fourth and sixth syllables from the end, i.e. alternating leftward from the penult. Monosyllabic nouns and verbs are stressed; articles, possessives, verbal particles, conjunctions and prepositions are unstressed; enclitic pronouns and a few words like Middle Cornish 'us' vary. George frames this historically: ultimate stress in early Brythonic shifted to the penult c. 1050; per Bailey's unpublished metrical work the stress-accent was penultimate while a pitch accent stayed on the final syllable, as in Welsh.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stated explicitly: 'a secondary stress fell on the fourth and sixth syllables from the end' (p. 507).
new_statements.exceptions: (1) Double stress in disyllables with primary on the second: loose compounds, noun + adjective (den bras 'big man'), noun + qualifier place-names (Penzance). (2) Antepenultimate stress: words of 3+ syllables containing an epenthetic vowel (banathel 'broom'), certain English loans (oratry). (3) Ultimate stress: shortened forms (yma 'there is', verbs in -he), many adverbs and prepositions (ynweth 'also', avel 'as'), compounds of war 'on' and negative na- (warnans 'downwards', nahen 'any other'), certain English loans (attes 'at ease'). Also a note that little direct textual evidence exists and the pattern is inferred from place-names and verse.
new_statements.identity_note: George describes the traditional language (Old, Middle and Late Cornish, extinct as a community language c. 1800), with stress inferred from place-names and Middle Cornish verse metrics; he says place-name evidence matches Breton (excluding Gwenedeg). Revived Cornish (Bock et al. 2010, held by the project) prescribes the same penultimate rule. The citation's 1st-edition page reference (1993, p. 430) was not verified: archive.org's 1993 copy (celticlanguages0000unse) is lending-restricted.

new_statements.quote: Double stress. In the following cases of disyllables, both syllables were stressed, the second bearing the primary stress: 1 loose compounds; 2 noun and adjective, e.g. den bras [ˌdɛːnˈbraːz] 'big man'; 3 place-names of the type noun + qualifier, e.g. Penzance [ˌpɛnˈzans]. Antepenultimate stress occurred in: 1 words of three syllables or more containing an epenthetic vowel, e.g. banathel [ˈbanaðəl] 'broom'; 2 certain loan-words from English, e.g. oratry [ˈɔratri]. Ultimate stress occurred in the following cases: 1 where longer forms had been shortened, e.g. yma [ɪˈmaː] 'there is, there are', verbs in -he; 2 numerous adverbs and prepositions, e.g. ynweth [ɪnˈwɛːð] 'also', avel [aˈvɛːl] 'as'

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: Coding fixed-strict penultimate (stress placement coded per word length as 10 010 1010 01010 (1 = a stressed syllable)) rests on George 2009:507 / 1993:430, the specialist reconstructive statement for an extinct language, and every source opened agrees on penultimate primary stress: StressTyp2 dump (George 1993:430, Pool 1958:6, Smith 1955:6) confirmed verbatim in the held SQL dump; held Toorians Middle Cornish grammar sec.1(c); held Jenner 1904 p.54; and four Cornish Language Partnership documents downloaded now (Bock et al. 2010 p.5; Bock 'basics' p.1). Nothing suggests the classification is wrong; the Williams/George 'prosodic shift' dispute concerns quantity/rhythm and pitch, not stress position. Two weaknesses keep it short of well-sourced: (1) the record's quote/cite/grade fields are empty and the deciding George text is not yet obtained (read at silo.pub, unsaved), so the verbatim p.507 check cannot be done in custody; (2) the secondary-stress clause (4th/6th from end)

sources.quote: "Stress normally falls on the last syllable but one (the 'penultima'). In loose compounds, primary stress falls on the second component, e.g. penn BLOODH. ... In close compounds, it falls regularly on the penultimate syllable. Following a convention established since the time of R. M. Nance, irregular or unpredictable stress has been marked in the glossary by inserting a dot after the stressed vowel."

sources.citation: Bock, Albert. n.d. (c.2008-2010). 'What the fuss is all about.. some basics of the Cornish reconstruction debate' [, kernewegva.com], 10 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: "Only two out of the three accentual features are clear: the second-last syllable in a word was normally the loudest (i.e. it was stressed) and, at the very least until the time of the Ordinalia, it was also the longest one. We have no idea if it also carried the highest pitch." Also frames the Williams 'Prosodic Shift' vs George debate as being about rhythm/length, not stress position.
